parsed.modern: 2. By some an opening is made in the side of the tube near the focus of the object-glass, through which the cross hairs are illuminated by means of a candle. But this method also is attended with inconveniences for the observer is incommoded by the light being so near his eyes, and the hairs themselves become liable to accidents through their exposed situation. An error also attends this method; which is, that, according to the position of the light illuminating these hairs, they will appear in different situations. For example, when the horizontal hair is enlightened above, we perceive a luminous line which may be taken for the hair itself, and which appears at its upper surface. On the other hand, when the hair is enlightened underneath, the luminous line will appear at the under surface of it; and the error will be the diameter of the hair, which often amounts to more than six seconds. M. de la Hire, however, found a remedy for this inconvenience. He often observed, that in moon-shine nights, when the weather was a little foggy, the cross hairs were distinctly seen; but when the heavens were serene, they could scarcely be perceived: he therefore covered with a piece of gauze, or fine silk-crape, that end of the tube next the object-glass; and this method succeeded so well, that a link placed at a good distance from the telescope to enlighten the crape, that the cross-hairs distinctly appeared, and the sight of the stars was by no means obscured.
